śaṅkha
(‘that which pacifies [evils]’)
------------------------------------------
The शङ्ख or conch is one of the common objects seen in the hands of images of many Hindu deities, especially those associated with विष्णु, and sometimes with the देवी.
The śaṅkha—according to the Brahmavaivartapurāṇa, Prakṛtikhaṇḍa chapter 18—was produced from the bones of the demon Śaṅkhacūḍa after he was killed by शिव.
There are two types of śaṅkhas: the vāmāvarta (spiralled from the left) and the dakṣiṇāvarta (spiralled from the right). The latter is considered extremely auspicious.
Sometimes four types of śaṅkhas are distinguished as suitable for the four varṇas.
White śaṅkhas are regarded as the best for use in worship.
Śaṅkhas are used in ritualistic worship of the deities and the water contained in them is considered extremely holy.
A śaṇkha may also be used to blow (and thus make sound which is auspicious to hear).
Warriors used to keep their own śaṅkhas and blow them loudly as a challenge thrown at the enemies.
The Bhagavadgītā (1.15, 16) gives the names of the śaṅkhas of कृष्ण (Pāñcajanya), अर्जुन (Devadatta) and others.
Śaṅkha is also the technical name for an immensely large number, one lakh crores (1012).
Śaṅkha and his brother लिखित were the authors of a well-known स्मृति that goes by their name.
One of the nine great treasures of कुबेर (the god of wealth) is known as शङ्ख.

saṅgīta
(‘well-sung; मुसिच्)
------------------------------------------
If drawing and painting can strike the eyes, सङ्गीत or मुसिच् has the power to rouse the heart. It has the potential to express the moral and spiritual sentiments to the highest degree. It is not only the medicine that can cure an aching heart but also help a spiritual aspirant to raise his सोउल् to God. That is why the Hindu sages have sometimes christened it as ‘nādayoga’ and God as ‘Nādabrahma’. And, मुसिच् has almost always allied itself with religion and spiritual values.
The three basic notes of Vedic chanting—udātta, अनुदात्त, and svarita—are the fundamental notes of Indian मुसिच्. These three notes developed later into seven in the Sāmaveda. They are: क्रुष्ट, prathama, dvitīya, tṛtīya, caturtha, mandra and atisvāra. They correspond to the notes pañcama (pa), madhyama (ma), गान्धार (ga), ऋषभ (ri), ṣaḍja (sa), daivata (da) and निषाद (ni), in modern Indian मुसिच्. Hence, the Sāmaveda has been considered to be the origin of Indian मुसिच्.
During the earliest period, सङ्गीत or मुसिच् was considered to be an integral part of nṛtya or nāṭya or dancing. Dancing, मुसिच् and drama (nāṭaka) were treated as one unit—Nāṭyaśāstra or the science of dramaturgy. And, भरत’s Nāṭyaśāstra (A.

) is considered to be the original systematic treatise on this subject. The other standard works often referred to are:
Saṅgītaratnamālā by Mammaṭa (A.

)
In Indian मुसिच् the two invariable basic notes are sa and pa. The others—ri, ga, ma, da and ni—are of two varieties each, making a total of 12 notes. Sometimes 16 notes are described, though, for all practical purposes 12 are enough.
A permutation and combination of these notes produce a variety of rāgas or tunes. Those tunes in which all the seven notes are present are called ‘melakartā’ or ‘janaka’ rāgas. The derivatives are known as ‘janya’ rāgas.
Veṅkaṭamakhi (A.

) in his magnum opus, the Caturdaṇḍiprakāśikā (written in Sanskrit verses) has grouped the 72 जनक-rāgas into two groups of 36 each. He has also dealt with many other fundamental aspects of मुसिच् in this great work which has remained as an invaluable guide to all musicians.
As far as the janya or the derived rāgas are concerned, they can be limitless. Even now, talented musicians are inventing new rāgas.
The various rāgas or tunes are capable of expressing a variety of feelings and sentiments such as love, anger, tenderness, sorrow, disappointment, pity, joy and so on.
Another speciality of Indian मुसिच् is that specific rāgas are assigned to specific periods of the day or night. If certain rāgas like Māyāmāḷava-gauḷa (or Bhairav) are to be sung early in the morning, Kalyāṇī (or Yaman) is to be sung in the night. The very atmosphere at that time is said to enhance its power to rouse the particular sentiment to which it is tuned.
If symphony is the heart of Western मुसिच्, śruti (drone or basic musical sound as the one produced by the tānpūra), राग (tune), ताल (fixed number of beats for each unit) and लय (uniform speed for the beats) are the basics for Indian मुसिच्. Thirty-five varieties of tālas have been evolved.
Though Indian मुसिच् had been one for several centuries, due to the Persian influence exerted during the Mughal period, there was a gradual branching into two schools: the uttarādi or the North Indian and the dakṣiṇādi or the South Indian (also called Carnāṭic). There are many similarities as also notable distinctions between the two schools. The uttarādi school further got subdivided into gharāṇās or traditions which are alive and active even today.
A मुसिच् performance is generally centred round the vocalist. In the South Indian classical मुसिच् the vocalist is accompanied by the violinist and another who plays on the mṛdaṅgam (a percussion instrument). Of course, the tānpūra should always be there as the basic instrument. Sometimes other percussion instruments like घटम् (a mud pot), khañjīra (a disc-like percussion instrument) and morsing (a small stringed instrument played by mouth) are also added.
In the North Indian classical मुसिच् performances, the vocalist is generally accompanied by the harmonium and the tabalā (a percussion instrument in two pieces) players. Occasionally stringed instruments (similar to the violin) like the sāraṅgī or the dilrūbā are also used. Tānpūra is, however, a must.
Apart from vocal मुसिच्, Indian मुसिच् system is rich in instruments too. Even in the Vedic and allied literature there are references to vīṇā (lute), vāṇa (an instrument with 100 strings), dhanurvīṇā, दुन्दुभि (drum), āḍambara and so on. The dhanurvīṇā is said to be the precursor of the violin now imported from the West. Many other instruments like bānsurī, flute, sitār, sarod, goṭuvādyam, pakhvāj, khol, clarionet, nādasvarm and shehanai have also come into use over the years.

sāṅkhya-yoga
(‘yoga of sāṅkhya [or knowledge]’)
------------------------------------------
The second chapter of the Bhagavad-gītā is called Sāṅkhyayoga since it deals with sāṅkhya (= ज्ञान) or knowledge of the आत्मन्.
Elsewhere (5.5), the words sāṅkhya and योग have been used to signify ज्ञान-योग and कर्मयोग.
The Prāṇāgnihotra Upaniṣad 1) uses the word to mean intense thinking.
In the Muktikopaniṣad (1.16) it means ज्ञानयोग.

Sāṅkhyakārikā
------------------------------------------
The Sāṅkhyadarśana or the Sāṅkhya philosophy is one of the six systems of Hindu philosophy. (See SĀṄKHYADARŚANA for details.)
The Sāṅkhyakārikā of ईश्वरकृष्ण (circa A.

to 450) is the most important and probably the earliest basic work of this system.
It is in the form of verses, 71 (or 73) in number, all in the āryā metre.
There are several Sanskrit commentaries—10 in all—on it, among which the following are more well-known:
Sāṅkhyakārikābhāṣya by गौडपाद.
Māṭharavṛtti or Māṭharabhāśya.
Jayamaṅgalā by one शङ्कर.
Sāṅkhyatattvakaumudī by वाचस्पति मिश्र (A.

)
Sāṅkhyacandrikā by नारायण Tīrtha.
All these commentaries consider the entire work as one unit running continuously. However one commentary has divided it into prakaraṇas and āhnikas as follows:
Prakaraṇas Āhnikas Kārikās
1 3 14
2 2 7
3 3 24
4 3 26
4 11 71

A brief summary of the work may now be attempted:
The first kārikā is introductory. The second stresses that knowledge (vijñāna) alone gives freedom from suffering.
Kārikās 3 to 8 describe the means of getting अपवर्ग (liberation).
Kārikās 9 to 14 establish the सत्कार्यवाद (See ASATKĀRYAVĀDA and SATKĀRYAVĀDA.) and describe the अव्यक्त or the प्रधान, the vyakta or the manifested products of the अव्यक्त, the three guṇas (sattva, रजस् and तमस्) and the पुरुष (the सोउल्).
Kārikās 15 to 21 deal with the अव्यक्त or प्रकृति as the original cause, its three guṇas as the constituents, multiplicity of the puruṣas or souls and that च्रेअतिओन् proceeds from their mutual association.
The next group of kārikās, 22 to 45, deals with the evolution of the प्रकृति into this universe through the 23 cosmic principles and their nature.
The last group, kārikās 46 to 71 (or 73) explain the various pariṇāmas or changes of बुद्धि (intellect), types of च्रेअतिओन् (which are threefold), the three worlds, role of प्रकृति in च्रेअतिओन् (which is only for helping the पुरुष or the सोउल् to get liberated), the nature of पुरुष as eternally free (never subject to any bondage in reality), the importance of tattvābhyāsa (repeated study of the funda-mental principles taught till now), लिबेरतिओन् and the jīvanmukta.
The treatise ends with the narration of the names of the great teachers of this tradition.
See also ĪŚVARAKṚṢṆA.

saṅghāta-śrāddha
(‘śrāddha in a group’)
------------------------------------------
Śrāddha (obsequial ceremony) is a compulsory religious rite performed for the benefit of the dead relatives.
Sometimes it may so happen that more than one relative may die on the same day though at different times. In such a case the śrāddhas for all of them are performed on the same day individually, one after the other, the order being the same as the order of their death.
If a group of relatives die together—as in the case of an accident—then the order depends on the nearness of the blood-relationship. For instance if a person’s wife, son, brother and paternal uncle meet with death at the same time, then the order of the śrāddhas would be for: the wife, son, brother and uncle one after the other.
Such śrāddhas are called ‘saṅghāta-śrāddha’.

Śaṅkha-लिखित-dharmasūtras
------------------------------------------
If the Śrutis (Vedas) deal with philosophical truths and occasionally refer to ethical principles and social conduct, the smṛtis or धर्मशास्त्रस् have codified and systematised these ethical principles as best as they could.
The Śaṅkha-लिखित-dharmasūtras is one such ancient work. It might have existed during the period 300 B. C. to A.

.
Śaṇkha and लिखित were brothers known for their pure life and uncompromising rectitude. (See LIKHITA for their story.)
The Dharmasūtra work attributed to them is not available now. From other sources which have quoted it, we can presume that it was a work in prose in the sūtra form.
The following works available now in print may be considered as the redacted condensations of the ancient original work:
Śaṅkhasmṛti — 330 verses in 18 chapters.
Likhitasmṛti — 93 verses.
Laghuśaṅkhasmṛti — 71 verses.
Śaṅkhalikhitasmṛti — 32 verses.

Out of these the first seems to be the oldest of the extant works.
Many well-known authors of धर्म-śāstras have quoted passages from शङ्ख or शङ्ख-लिखित or लिखित.
Not much is known about the actual contents of this ancient work. However, this work seems to have been more liberal in its social attitudes like allowing नियोग (levirate) and permitting a ब्राह्मण to marry girls from all the four varṇas.

saṅkalpa
(‘religious declaration’)
------------------------------------------
In हिन्दुइस्म्, practically every religious act or rite has to be preceded by a सङ्कल्प. It is actually a declaratory formula giving not only the details of the day according to the पञ्चाङ्ग (traditional चलेन्दर्) but also the purpose behind the act.
A typical saṅkalpamantra should contain the names and other details of the कल्प, मन्वन्तर, yuga, geographical position of the place of performance, year, solstice, month, fortnight, date and day of the week, as also the name of the person who is performing and the purpose.
Any rite not preceded by such a सङ्कल्प will become fruitless.
See KALPA, MANVANTARA and YUGAS.

------------------------------------------
Introduction
When धर्म (righteousness) abandons its followers because they have ignored it or distorted it, and, अधर्म (villainy) quickly fills its place, masquerading, perhaps, as a better substitute, God is obliged to intervene! (vide Bhagavadgītā 4.7, 8) He may do so either by directly descending to this earth as an अवतार (incarnation) or by infilling certain chosen persons to accomplish his task of restoring the balance in favour of the former.
ŚaṅkarācāryaDuring the period preceding the advent of शङ्कर (also known as Śaṅkarācārya), the Sanātana-धर्म (the Ancient and Eternal Religion, now commonly known as हिन्दुइस्म्) based on the वेदस्, was facing stiff opposition from several quarters.
Buddhism with its śūnyavāda (nihilism), जैनिस्म् with its śyādvāda or अनेकान्तवाद (which states that a thing can be described in several ways, thus leading to greater confusion), Cārvāka schools (materialism that denied the existence of all non-temporal objects), the कापालिक and the वामाचार cults which propagated unethical and abominable practices in the name of religion—everyone of these was trying to shake the foundation of हिन्दुइस्म्.
It was at such a critical period of the Vedic religion, which badly needed a true and staunch follower to restore it to its former glory, that शङ्कर was born.
Life in Brief
Any attempt to portray the life of शङ्कर runs into two genuine difficulties. Firstly, the available material is too meagre to fix his date. Secondly, the traditional biographies (all in Sanskrit) are so full of miracles attributed to him that it is difficult to accept them or explain them in any logical way.
Though almost all biographies agree that शङ्कर lived just for 32 years, the year of his birth varies from 508 B. C. up to A.
. The most widely accepted year is A.
. However some scholars push it back to A.

also.
About 21 works that generally go by the name Śaṅkaravijaya or Śaṅkara-digvijaya dealing with शङ्कर’s life in detail—have so far been discovered. Out of these, the ones by आनन्दगिरि (Śaṅkara-vijaya) and by Mādhava-विद्यारण्य (Śaṅkaradigvijaya) are considered more authoritative and widely accepted.
Śaṅkara’s life as given in these texts may now be summarised as follows:
Śivaguru and Āryāmbā were a deeply pious couple belonging to the well-known नम्बूदिरि caste, living in कालडी (or Kālaṭī) (the modern town of Kalady in the Kerala State) situated on the bank of the river Pūrṇā. This childless couple got शङ्कर as their son after much prayer and supplication to Lord शिव of Vṛṣabhā-cala (a hillock near कालडी, the deity being known as Candramoulīśvara).
As indicated by the Lord, the boy would become an omniscient spiritual giant, but his life would be of short duration.
Śaṅkara was extraordinarily brilliant and mastered all the śāstras (scriptural and other treatises) taught to him even at a young age.
Unfortunately, ड़थेर् Śivaguru died soon, leaving शङ्कर entirely to the care of his मोथेर् Āryāmbā.
Being indrawn by temperament and having realised the transitory nature of the world, through the direct experience of the death of his ड़थेर्, शङ्कर decided to embrace सṁन्यास (monastic life). The only impediment in the path was the मोथेर्’s love and attachment, and the need to take her permission!
By a quirk of destiny, this came about sooner than expected. One day when he was taking bath in the river Pūrṇā, a big crocodile caught him. As he was struggling for life, and finding that he was waging a losing battle, he appealed to his wailing मोथेर् who was standing on the bank, to give him permission to take सṁन्यास mentally and die in peace. सṁन्यास taken just before death.">1 She had no alternative but to oblige. However, the crocodile left him as mysteriously as it had caught him. As per the scriptural injunctions, he now had to take formal सṁन्यास. Most unwillingly the मोथेर् gave him the permission to do so, but with a rider that he should be by her bedside at the time of her death.
He was just eight years at that time!
Having heard that Govindabhagavat-pāda, a very great monk (considered an अवतार or इन्चर्नतिओन् of the Great Serpent, आदिशेष) was living on the bank of the river नर्मदा in a cave, शङ्कर hurried there. The great teacher too was eagerly awaiting this extraordinary disciple whose arrival he had already known through his yogic vision.
After a vigorous training spread over three years शङ्कर was commanded to go to काशी, the heart of all learning—sacred and secular.
As he settled down in काशी for some time, preaching his doctrine of Advaita Vedānta, he gathered a number of disciples, among whom Sanandana—later well-known as पद्मपाद, one of the four chief disciples—was one.
A strange encounter here with an untouchable—who was none other than Lord Viśvanātha (Śiva) himself—removed the last vestige of इग्नोरन्चे from his मिन्द्, making him a perfect being and a perfect teacher.
As directed by शिव, शङ्कर proceeded to बदरीनाथ, the famous पिल्ग्रिमगे centre in the हिमालयस्, where he renovated the old temple of नारायण, instituted proper modes of ritualistic worship and then started writing his (now celebrated) commentary on the Brahma-sūtras. This is said to have been fully approved and appreciated by its original author, the sage व्यास himself.
Later on, he moved towards South India, vanquishing and converting many a scholar, among whom the greatest was मण्डन मिश्र. According to some of the traditional biographers, it was this मण्डन मिश्र who became the saṁnyāsin सुरेश्वर, though quite a few scholars do not subscribe to this view.
Among those who were converted to Vedic modes of life and worship were the Kāpālikas of Śrīśaila (now in Andhra Pradesh) and the गाणपत्यस् of गोकर्ण (in Karnataka), both of whom were following some abominable practices.
It was again during this sojourn that he added two more distinguished saṁnyāsin disciples to his retinue, हस्तामलक and Toṭaka.
Meanwhile, he learnt that his मोथेर् was on her deathbed, hurried to her and gave her a vision of Lord विष्णु before she passed away. He also personally cremated her body much to the chagrin of the local residents and relatives who were against him.
During this period, पद्मपाद irretrievably lost the manuscript of his gloss on the commentary of शङ्कर on the Brahmasūtras. However, शङ्कर redeemed from memory that part of it which had been read out to him earlier by पद्मपाद himself. (This unfinished work is now known as Pañcapādikā and has been printed.)
After completing the successful tour of the South, शङ्कर now journeyed to the north right upto Kāśmīra (Kashmir), vanquished all the scholars and occupied the Sarvajñapīṭha, the seat meant for the greatest scholar, in the temple of सरस्वती, the goddess of learning.
During his sojourn round the country, शङ्कर had established four Maṭhas or monasteries in the four cardinal points at पुरी, Śṛṅgerī, Dvāraka and Joṣimaṭha. He anointed his four chief disciples as their heads, to carry on his work even after his demise, thus creating a great monastic tradition.
The following table gives the details:
No. Name Place First Pontiff
1. Śāradā Maṭha Śṛṅgerī Sureśvara
2. Kālikā Maṭha Dvārakā Hastāmalaka
3. Jyotirmaṭha Badarī Toṭaka
4. Govardhana Maṭha Purī Padmapāda

By this time he had firmly re-established the Vedic religion by his written works, vigorous propaganda of its principles and leaving behind him a band of illustrious disciples as also religious (monastic) institutions.
He is said to have entered into a cave in the हिमालयस् near Badarī—known as the Dattātreyaguhā—and disappeared forever.
According to another version current even now, शङ्कर is said to have established another मठ at काञ्चीपुरम् (in Tamil Nadu) (called Kāmakoṭipīṭha) and lived there for the rest of his life until his demise, which also took place there only. The controversy regarding this has not yet been resolved due to the non-availability of clinching evidence.
His Works
Śaṅkara was a prolific writer. He has left behind him a voluminous literature which can be categorised into three groups: Bhāṣyas; Prakaraṇas; and, Stotras.
Bhāṣyas are his erudite expositions of the basic works on Vedānta philosophy and Hindu religion. Apart from the ten उपनिषद्स्, the Brahamasūtras and the Bhagavadgītā (collectively called the प्रस्थानत्रय), he has written bhāṣyas on the Viṣṇusahasranāma (vide Mahā-bhārata, Anuśāsanparva, ch. 149), the Sanatsujātīya (Udyogaparva, ch. 40-45) and the Lalitātriśatī also.
As regards the prakaraṇas which are simple treatises on Advaita Vedānta, quite a large number of them have been attributed to him. Of them, the following works are popular: Aparokṣānubhūti, Ātmabodha, Laghuvākyavṛtti, Upadeśa-sāhasrī, Vākyavṛtti and Vivekacūdāmaṇi
A very large number of stotras or hymns, on almost all the well-known deities of the Hindus, are ascribed to him. It is rather difficult to segregate a few and declare that they are definitely his. However, the following stotras are definitely his compositions according to scholars seasoned in शङ्कर’s style of writing as also other available evidence: Ānanda-laharī, Bhajagovindastotra, Dakṣiṇā-mūrtyaṣṭaka, Daśaślokī, Gopālāṣṭaka, Harimīḍestotra, Manīṣāpañcaka, Śiva-bhujaṅgaprayāta, Sopānapañcaka and Viṣṇuṣaṭpadī.
Apart from these, two works on tantra—the Prapañcasāra and the Saundaryalaharī—are also attributed to him.
His Philosophy
Śaṅkara being the greatest propagator of Advaita Vedānta, holds the view that the basic truth or reality behind this universe of multiplicity, of myriad names and forms, is one and one only, advaita, the one without a second. This reality called ब्रह्मन् appears as the many due to the peculiar, indefinable, factor called māyā. Just as semidarkness hides the real nature of a rope (lying on the road) as rope and projects in it a snake (as it appears to us then) which is not there, so also māyā hides the true nature of ब्रह्मन् (as Sat-Cit-आनन्द, existence-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्-bliss) and projects on that base, this manifold universe. Even as a bright light reveals the rope as rope, dispelling the snake-appearance, thereby removing all fear, in the same way, ज्ञान or right knowledge removes the इल्लुसिओन् brought about by māyā.
Though शङ्कर has not defined and explained māyā in detail, he has given enough indications in his writings that it acts like an existing positive force (bhāvarūpa) but disappears mysteriously once it is neutralised by ज्ञान (knowledge or direct experience).
Once this basic standpoint that this multiple universe is a projection of māyā on ब्रह्मन् is accepted, शङ्कर is prepared to give it a greater degree of reality (called vyāvahārikasattā or empirical reality), because, then only the reverse process of attenuating and eliminating it is possible. Otherwise the whole structure of sādhana based on this empirical reality collapses!
It is at this secondary level (of empirical reality) that शङ्कर concedes the process of च्रेअतिओन् of the world as given in the उपनिषद्स्, the multiplicity and limited nature of the jīvas (bound souls), ईश्वर (God, ब्रह्मन् in the garb of the Creator) as responsible for the च्रेअतिओन्, sustenance and dissolution of the world and the entire process of sādhana by the jīvas to regain their lost (essential) nature.
As a corollary, शङ्कर also acknowledges that māyā has its individual counterpart, generally called अविद्या or अज्ञान (ignorance, nescience). It is this अविद्या that makes a जीव (the individual) feel identified with the body-मिन्द् complex, see the external world of duality, feel attraction or repulsion towards its objects, work to get what he wants, thus getting into the bondage of the cycle of births and deaths.
Once this जीव awakens and takes to the path of sādhana and realises his true nature as sat-cit-आनन्द, the आत्मन् (the Self or the सोउल्), his अविद्या is totally dispelled.
The body may continue to function for some time due to prārabdha कर्म. When it falls, he is fully liberated, being merged in ब्रह्मन्, never to be born again.
The individual who realises his आत्मन्-nature and continues to live in the embodied state till the prārabdha expires, is called a jīvanmukta (‘the liberated, even while living’). In this state his subjective reactions to the world have totally changed though he continues to see the world as before. The man, who has discovered the rope as rope in good light, will continue to see it as a snake in semidarkness, since the cause of the इल्लुसिओन् is outside himself. However, his personal reaction to it has totally changed from one of fear to that of indifference or even amusement.
Epilogue
If शङ्कर is fondly remembered even today—twelve centuries after his advent—both by the intellectual classes and the simple masses—it is not a little due to his all-round personality. His bhāṣyas and prakaraṇas have enriched the knowledge of the former. His stotras on various deities commonly worshipped by the latter, have infilled them with devotion. The various miracles he is said to have performed—like the raining of golden myrobalans in the होउसे of the poor lady or changing the course of the Pūrṇā river to facilitate bathing by his aged mother—restored faith in the power of तपस् (austerity) and divine grace in the minds of the sceptics. By putting a stop to the bizarre practices that were being carried out in the name of religion by certain sects and cults, and converting their votaries to purer ways of life, he saved them and the society too. His convincing victories over the non-Vedic and anti-Vedic religions restored the Vedic religion to its pristine glory. The reorganisation of Hindu मोनस्तिचिस्म् made it more people-oriented through his direction, viz., pravāsa (touring) and pracāra (preaching).
Finally, his tender affection towards his lonely मोथेर् and the filial duty he discharged (fulfilling his promise) towards her during her last moments, speaks volumes of the intensely human aspect of his personality.
He did all these things and much more, never for a moment lowering his own dignity of demeanor or slipping from the sublime heights of monastic life.
Only an avatārapuruṣa (an इन्चर्नतिओन् of God) can accomplish such feats.
See also ADVAITA VEDANTA DARŚANA.

Sāṅkhya Darśana
------------------------------------------
Introduction
After stating his views and defending them with the help of appropriate quotations from the उपनिषद्स्, बादरायण in his Brahmasūtras starts his criticisms of other schools with the Sāṅkhya philosophy (

-820) has given the reason as to why the Sāṅkhya system was chosen first. The word he has used (‘pradhāna-malla-nibarhaṇa-nyāyena,’ ‘by the maxim of overcoming the chief wrestler’) is very significant. If a well-known wrestler overcomes the chief wrestler of the opponents’ group first, it is as good as all the others also being vanquished, even without fighting them! This shows how important a system साङ्ख्य दर्शन is.
As per the orthodox accounts, this system was founded by the sage कपिल (vide Bhāgavata 3.25-33). The work that has come down to us, as his, is the Sāṅkhyasūtras. It is obviously a late work. It is in six chapters and contains 526 sūtras in all. विज्ञानभिक्षु (16th century A. D.) has written a commentary on the same, known as Sāṅkhya-pravacana-bhāṣya.
The Sāṅkhyan tradition of philosophy was nourished and propagated by कपिल’s disciple आसुरि and his disciple पञ्चशिख. Some sūtras of पञ्चशिख are found quoted in the Vyāsabhāṣya (A.

) on the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.). The complete work as such has not yet been found.
By far, the earliest available (and reliable) work on the Sāṅkhya is the Sāṅkhyakārikās of ईश्वरकृष्ण (5th century A. D.). It has 70 stanzas (in the āryā metre) and hence, sometimes, designated as Sāṅkhya-saptati also.
It contains a brief but brilliant and lucid exposition of the doctrines.
This work has two well-known commentaries: Sāṅkhyakārikā-bhāṣya of गौडपाद (A.

).
The Sāṅkhyasāra of विज्ञानभिक्षु and the Sāṅkhyapravacanasūtravṛtti of अनिरुद्ध (15th cent. A. D.) are the other works of importance.
Significance of the Name
The origin of the word ‘Sāṅkhya’ seems to have been an enigma. Some thinkers derive it from saṅkhyā (= number) and opine that it might have got this name since it enumerates the ultimate principles in च्रेअतिओन् as 25. Others however think that since it stresses ज्ञान or knowledge as the only means of लिबेरतिओन् and since ‘saṅkhyā’ means ज्ञान (samyak khyāyate), the word fits in very well with the system.
The प्रमाणस् or Methods of Knowledge
Unlike many other systems, the Sāṅkhya accepts only three प्रमाणस् or valid sources of knowledge. They are प्रत्यक्ष (direct perception), अनुमान (inference) and शब्द (testimony).
Pratyakṣa is the direct चोग्नितिओन् of an object through its contact with a sense-organ, like the eyes seeing a table or the ears hearing the chirping of birds. The first contact may give a general knowledge. This is called ‘nirvikalpaka’ (indeterminate). When, on closer observation and thinking, the perception gives a clearer idea, it is called ‘savikalpaka’ (determinate). On seeing a table, the first reaction is, ‘I am seeing some object.’ Then comes a clearer idea, ‘This is a wooden table with a red cloth spread over it.’ The first is निर्विकल्पक-प्रत्यक्ष and the second, सविकल्पक-प्रत्यक्ष.
Anumāna or inference is the second source of knowledge. It is gained by seeing some sign first and then inferring the reality behind it. The stock example given by most of the philosophers is, coming to the conclusion that there is fire on a distant hill, by seeing smoke rising out of it. Since our previous experience through direct perception has shown that wherever there is smoke, there is fire, here also we conclude that there is fire, even though we do not see it directly. An invariable concomitance between the object seen and the unseen object inferred (here, the smoke and the fire) is a necessary precondition.
Śabda or testimony is the third and the last of the प्रमाणस्. It is the testimony of a reliable person. This is called laukika-शब्द or āptavākya. The Sāṅkhya, however, does not recognise this as a separate pramāṇa since it depends upon the perception and inference of that reliable person. It is the testimony of the Śruti or the वेदस् that the Sāṅkhya philosophy admits as the independent and last pramāṇa. The वेदस् give us true knowledge about the supersensuous realities, which cannot otherwise be known, by प्रत्यक्ष or अनुमान. The वेदस् being apauruṣeya (not man-made but divine), are infallible. They embody the intuitions of the great ṛṣis, the enlightened sages.
The Prameyas or the Objects to be Known
Adopting the principle of “from the seen to the unseen or from the known to the unknown,” Sāṅkhyan metaphysics has reduced all the realities in our experience to two fundamental and eternal substances: the प्रकृति (also called प्रधान and अव्यक्त) (the insentient nature, the matrix of all lifeless and unconscious objects); the पुरुष (the being, the conscious self or the सोउल्).
The basic argument behind this conclusion is called ‘Satkāryavāda,’ the principle that the effect (= कार्य) pre-existed (= sat) in the cause (= कारण), before manifestation. For instance, when a pot is prepared out of clay, the pot already existed in the clay, though in a potential form. The main लोगिच् behind this is that something can never be produced out of nothing.
Applying this argument to the world of our experience where every object is seen to possess three characters—pleasure, pain and indifference—the Sāṅkhya comes to the conclusion that there must be three basic subtle substances from which these three characters are derived. It calls them as guṇas—sattvaguṇa (producing pleasure or happiness), rajoguṇa (producing pain and suffering) and tamoguṇa (producing neither).
Each of these guṇas stands for a distinct aspect of physical reality. सत्त्व signifies whatever is pure and fine, and, conduces to the production of knowledge as also happiness. रजस् is ever active. It is also responsible for desires and ambitions, to fulfil which one has to actively work. तमस् is stolid and offers resistance. It tends to sleep and inactivity.
These three guṇas always exist together and can never get separated. When these three—which are ever in turmoil as it were—are in a perfectly balanced state, not interfering with one another, though ever active or in perpetual motion within themselves, constitute the प्रकृति or प्रधान. In other words, प्रकृति is none other than these three guṇas in a state of perfect balance.
This प्रकृति is the basic material, primal matter, from which the universe evolves. It is ‘jaḍa,’ i.e., it has no चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्.
The पुरुष (the सोउल्) on the other hand is a conscious entity; nay, चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् is his very essence. He is eternal, ever pure, ever detached (asaṅga) and all-pervading. There are innumerable puruṣas or souls, as many as the living beings.
Evolution of the World
The च्रेअतिओन् or evolution of the world has its starting point in the saṁyoga or effective contact between the पुरुष and the प्रकृति. The totality of the karmas (unseen deserts) of the puruṣas disturbs the balance of the guṇas in प्रकृति and sets in motion the process of evolution.
Since प्रकृति is jaḍa (lifeless and devoid of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्) and the पुरुष is asaṅga (absolutely unattached) how can they ever co-operate in this process of च्रेअतिओन्? Such co-operation is possible even as a blind man and a lame man can team together to come out of a forest, the blind one carrying the lame person who can now direct him on the right road!
Another example given by the Sāṅkhyas is that of the spontaneous flow of milk from the udder of the मोथेर् cow when its calf is nearby.
The process of evolution from प्रकृति is as follows: As a result of the guṇas mixing with one another, the first evolute coming out of the प्रकृति is the महत् or the बुद्धि (the cosmic intellect). From that emerges अहङ्कार (cosmic ego, the principle of individuation). From the sāttvik part of अहङ्कार evolve मनस् (cosmic मिन्द्), the five ज्ञानेन्द्रियस् (cosmic organs of knowledge like the eyes and the ears) and the five कर्मेन्द्रियस् (cosmic organs of action like the hands and the feet). From the tāmasik part of अहङ्कार are produced the five तन्मात्रस् (subtle elements of earth, water etc.) and from them, further, evolve the five महाभूतस् or gross elements (of earth, water, fire, air and ether).
In all, including the प्रकृति, there will now be 24 cosmic principles or elements. The rest of च्रेअतिओन् takes place by their permutation and combination, each पुरुष getting involved with a psycho-physical complex (body) as per his कर्म.
Bondage and Liberation
It is interesting to note here that according to the Sāṅkhyan metaphysics the very purpose of the evolution of the प्रकृति into this world is to give the पुरुष one more chance for लिबेरतिओन्. Again, it is the same प्रकृति and its evolute, the world, that binds him once more!
The main cause of bondage of the पुरुष and his consequent suffering in the world is aviveka (ignorance, non-discrimination between himself as pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and प्रकृति which is jaḍa, the unconscious entity). It is this that is leading him from birth to death, or from life to life ad infinitum.
The question as to how and when he got into this mess can never be answered, except by stating that it is anādi (beginningless) but sānta (has an end).
Since aviveka or इग्नोरन्चे is responsible for this bondage, कैवल्य or लिबेरतिओन् can come only from विवेकख्याति or right knowledge. ‘Khyāti’ means know-ledge (in the sense of direct experience) and ‘viveka’ means separating himself as the पुरुष, the pure conscious entity, from the प्रकृति, the insentient matter. This can be attained by following the eight steps of योग wherein the पुरुष or the सोउल् is the object of meditation.
The साङ्ख्य दर्शन accepts two kinds of लिबेरतिओन्: जीवन्मुक्ति and videha-मुक्ति. The former is attained even while living here, the body continuing to live for some more time, till the prārabdha-कर्म (the कर्म that was responsible for starting this life) is exhausted. In this state, the perfect man continues to live in the world, though not of the world.
The final लिबेरतिओन् comes after the death of the body—that is why it is called ‘videhamukti’—and the person will never come back to this mundane world. He will attain the state perfectly free from all pain and suffering, though there is no experience of bliss. However, since चैतन्य or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् is his essence, he will ever remain in his own state.

Saṅkarṣaṇa
(‘one who was drawn’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the names of बलराम, elder brother of कृष्ण. He was the seventh baby in the womb of देवकी from Vasu-deva. However, योगमाया, the mysterious power of Lord विष्णु, drew the foetus from the womb of देवकी and placed it in the womb of रोहिणी, the first wife of Vasudeva who was then living in Nandagokula. Hence बलराम got this name. (Saṅkarṣaṇa literally means ‘well-drawn’.)
See BALARĀMA for details.

-1568)
------------------------------------------
Life
Śaṅkaradeva is the brightest star of the Vaiṣṇava Movement in Assam and north-east India, whose contribution is no less than that of श्रीकृष्ण चैतन्य (A.

-1533) in Bengal and Orissa.
He was born at the village Ālipukhuri (Nowgong district, Assam). His parents were Kusumbara and Satyasandhā. He lost his parents very early in life and was brought up by his grandparents. He got a good एदुचतिओन् in a Sanskrit school and also developed his god-given talents in मुसिच्, painting and composing poems.
He was married and had a daughter. His wife died immediately afterwards.
He went out (when he was thirty-three) on a long पिल्ग्रिमगे and travel spread over twelve years. He visited many places including काशी, वृन्दाबन्, मथुरा, कुरुक्षेत्र, द्वारका and रामेश्वरम्. During these visits, the strong current of वैष्णविस्म् he noticed everywhere due to the influence of saintly poets like विद्यापति (15th century A. D.), जयदेव (12th century A. D.) and श्रीकृष्ण Caitanya—whom he met for a short period—practically converted him from his शाक्त moorings to the Vaiṣṇava creed.
After returning to his place he was forced by his close relatives to marry a second time. This perturbed him much. However, the chance arrival of Jagadīśa-mitra—a great pundit and a travelling mendicant—helped him to regain his balance and peace. Jagadīśamitra stayed with him and taught him the Bhāgavata. शङ्करदेव’s चोन्वेर्सिओन् to वैष्णविस्म् was now complete. This inspired him to translate the Daśamaskandha (the tenth book of the Bhāgavata containing कृष्ण’s story in great detail) into the Kāmarūpī (Assamese) language, in simple verses.
Recurring political troubles forced him to migrate to safer places, finally settling down at Belguri on the bank of the stream Dhoasuti in North Lakhimpur (Assam).
Cult
Though शङ्करदेव adopted Vaiṣṇa-vism as his religion he evolved his own form of it and developed a cult. He carved a wooden image of कृष्ण, called it Madanagopāla and established it in his prayer-hall with elaborate ceremonies. The prayer-hall itself was called ‘nāmaghar’.
He started his own form of initiation called ‘śaraṇa’. This had three categories or aspects: nāmaśaraṇa, guruśaraṇa and bhaktiśaraṇa a la Buddhist śaraṇas (Buddha, धर्म and Saṅgha).
In other prayer-halls built under his supervision or guidance, he installed the भागवत-book instead of कृष्ण’s image on a wooden pedestal. This new method averted the need for formal worship, that too only by a ब्राह्मण, and associated rituals. All devotees, irrespective of caste or religion, could offer a simple service to the book before congregational prayers called kīrtan.
The simple process of initiation he adopted was to transmit the मन्त्र hare कृष्ण, hare rāma.
The Bhāgavata was adopted not only as the scripture but also as the object of worship.
Philosophy
According to शङ्करदेव, कृष्ण is the Supreme God who is a person (Puruṣa, पुरुषोत्तम, परमेश्वर and Nārā-yaṇa), eternal, omniscient and omnipotent. The puruṣas (or jīvas, individual souls) are many and are His aṁśas or parts (vide Bhagavadgītā 15.7). The insentient प्रकृति (nature) is also his.
Śaṅkaradeva lays great stress on भक्ति, that too dāsyabhakti (considering oneself as a dāsa or servant of God). The most important aspect of this is ekaśaraṇatva (total surrender or dedication to God).
Though मोक्ष or salvation (freedom from transmigratory existence) is accepted, the devotee is indifferent to it since he enjoys devotion to God much more.
Works
Śaṅkaradeva did not write commentaries on the प्रस्थानत्रय (See PRASTHĀNATRAYA.). But he has left quite a few works for the posterity. They are: Bhaktiratnākara (in Sanskrit); Kīrtana (in simple verses suited to मुसिच्); Guṇamālā (a synopsis of the Bhāgavata); Aṅkiā-nāṭ (one-act dramas); a translation of a part of Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa; a number of devotional songs known as bargīts (varagītā, ‘excellent songs’). Except the first, all the other works are in the Kāmārūpī or Assamese language.
Mention should be made here of the work Nāmaghoṣa by his chief disciple Mādhavadeva, which gained great respect from the followers and became popular.
Epilogue
The भक्ति-movement he started gradually spread in the whole area. However, it also split into six major groups in course of time.
Institutions known as satras also came into being, associated with this movement. (See SATRAS for details.)

saṅgava
(‘when the cows are gathered together [for milking]’)
------------------------------------------
A day of 24 hours is divided into 30 muhūrtas, one मुहूर्त being equal to 48 minutes. The day-time has 15 muhūrtas. This period is divided into five equal parts: prātaḥ or udaya (sunrise); सङ्गव (milking time); madhyāhna (midday); aparāhṇa (afternoon); sāyāhna (evening). Each of these is of 144 minutes’ (or 2 hours and 24 minutes) duration.
The second part is called सङ्गव because that is the time the cows are gathered together and milked.
Saṅgava is also suitable for prātar-होम (morning offering of oblations into the sacred fire) and for entering into a vrata (taking certain vows).
The प्रवर्ग्य rite (See PRAVARGYA for details.) is to be performed during this time.
Some धर्मशास्त्रस् (vide Gṛhya-sūtras of Hiraṇyakeśin) consider this period of the day as suitable for मर्रिअगे ceremonies also.

According to another version, he was a disciple of शङ्कर himself and adorned the Kāmakoṭipīṭha (now at काञ्चीपुरम्)—a monastery of advaita tradition, said to have been established by Śaṅkara—as its second pontiff.
The Saṅkṣepaśārīraka closely follows the commentary of शङ्कर on the Brahmasūtras.
It is in four chapters, written in verses of different metres, as follows:
First Chapter — 563 verses
Second Chapter — 248 verses
Third Chapter — 365 verses
Fourth Chapter — 63 verses
Total — 1239 verses

The first chapter describes ब्रह्मन् as the pure and ultimate cause of everything through अज्ञान (nescience). This अज्ञान rests on the pure self, operates on it as its viṣaya or object, covering its essential nature and creating delusory appearances. It is in the सुषुप्ति or the deep-sleep state that pure bliss, untainted by sorrow, is experienced.
The second chapter further elucidates the doctrines dealt with in the first. There is also a refutation of other schools like Sāṅkhya and न्याय.
The third chapter deals with the sādhanas, or means of destroying अज्ञान and prepare oneself for the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्. The last chapter describes the nature of emancipation.

Śāṅkhāyana Gṛhyasūtras
------------------------------------------
The गृह्यसूत्रस् are a subsidiary of the Vedāṅga known as the कल्पसूत्रस्. They deal primarily with the rites connected with the home and family-life.
The Śāṅkhāyana Gṛhyasūtras belongs to the Ṛgveda. It is a fairly long work. There are 1075 sūtras accommodated in 96 khaṇḍas or sections, which again, are contained in 6 adhyāyas or chapters.
The contents may be briefly summarised as follows:
Sacrifices like the pākayajñas and the दर्शपूर्णमास; details of the सṁस्कारस् or sacraments like विवाह (marriage), पुṁसवन, जातकर्म and so on, including उपनयन and उपाकर्म; duties of a स्नातक (one who has completed his Vedic एदुचतिओन्); building a होउसे and the rituals connected with entering it (called गृहप्रवेश); śrāddhas (obsequial rites); पिल्ग्रिमगे and Vedic sacrificial fire; consecration of wells, ponds, tanks and gardens; prāyaścittas or expiations.
For details of these subjects, see under the respective titles.

Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka
------------------------------------------
This is a part of the Śāṅkhāyana Brāhmaṇa, which is better known as Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa.
This Āraṇyaka follows the Aitareya Āraṇyaka closely.
There are 15 adhyāyas or chapters containing 137 khaṇḍas or sections.
The first two adhyāyas deal with the Vedic rite called महाव्रत. (See MAHĀ-VRATAf or details.)
The sixth adhyāya refers to the countries or areas such as उशीनर, Matsya, काशी, Videha and Kurupāñcāla.
The thirteenth adhyāya contains much material taken from the Bṛhadā-raṇyaka Upaniṣad.
The long list of teachers given includes the names of कहोल Kauṣītaki, उद्दालक आरुणि, सोम Prātiveśya and others who are found in the उपनिषद्स् also.

Śāṅkhāyana
------------------------------------------
Śāṅkhāyana is an ancient sage. His name is sometimes spelt as (or identified with) Sāṅkhyāyana also. He belongs to the Bāṣkalaśākhā of the Ṛgveda. He was perhaps known as Suyajña-शाङ्खायन too.
The Taittirīyaprātiśākhya (15.7) mentions his name along with that of Kāṇḍamāyana.
The Bhāgavata mentions one Sāṅkhyāyana as a disciple of Sanatkumāra and who was a परमहṁस himself. He spread the institution of सṁन्यास.
An Āraṇyaka, a ब्राह्मण and a Śrautasūtra have been attributed to his authorship. However, the full text of his गृह्यसूत्रस् is available now.
See ŚĀṄKHĀYANA GṚHYASŪTRAS for details.
